entries.english:
Count Ulric von Viten sells to Gerard, Bishop of Trent, all his allodial lands situated in that bishopric. (From the original.) Done at Trent, 5 January 1231.

In the year of the Lord 1231, in the fourth indiction, on the fifth day of January, at Trent, in a chamber of the palace, in the presence of the lords, the dean of the Holy Church of Trent, the Count of Tyrol, Adelper and Berthold, brothers of Wanga, Nicolaus of Egna, Ulric of Beseno, Duringus of Formiano, Jeremias of Castelnuovo, Rudolf Scanzig, Bertold of Cagno, Riprandus and Otto Richi, Ulric of Rambaldo, Zackei, Heinrich de Porta, Gotefred de Porta, Peregrinus Wichomarius, Tridentinus son of the late Rudolf Rubeus, Rolandus, Otto Grassi, Gunselmus, Aychebonus, Ainzo of Saint Peter, Malapeza, Tocolinus, Otolinus Gandi, Maraldus, judge of Trent, Ecelinus, judge, Arnold of Arso, Peregrinus the notary, Oluridinus the notary, and many other witnesses called for the purpose, Lord Count Ulric of Ultimis, by right and in the capacity of a sale of allodial property for allodial property and in return for an allod free and clear, enfeoffed Lord Gerard, by the grace of God Bishop of the Church of Trent, who received it for his church and bishopric, with all his mazinates and the people belonging to those mazinates, male and female, together with all the movable property they have or may acquire and all their children and descendants, present or future, and with all his vassals from his allodial holdings which they hold as fiefs from him in the Bishopric of Trent, and in the march, county, and duchy, as well as all the allodial properties which the Count holds in the Bishopric of Trent.

Among those included, he assigned the following noble people of his noble macinata, all knights by birth: Lord Ulric the Seneschal of Gurlano and his sister with ten sons; Heinrich of Mareto with seven sons and his wife; Johannes and his sister of Castelvecchio with seven sons; Nichilinus with his brother and sister of Castelvecchio; Lady Sophia of Bugnango with her three sons; Ardoinus of Puzillo, half; Ulric Chirkrius with his four sons, half; Heinrich Chirkerius with three sons, half; another son of his, half; Waiferius of Conalano with one daughter; the wife of Ulric of Ultimis with nine sons, whose sons belong by half to Count Ulric of Piano; Federicus of Flones and his mother; Eberardus of Tuene with his wife and five sons; the sister of Nihilinus with four sons, whose sons belong by half to the Count of Tyrol; the sons of Penzena of Tisens; two sons of Ardoinus, one of whom belongs to Count Heinrich; Lady Mulilda with four sons, who belong by half to Count Egenonus; Heinrich of Tisens with his wife and three sons; the daughter of Ulric, half, born of the daughter of Otto of Tisens; Heinrich Nonerius with nine sons, whose sons belong by half to Count Egenonus; Ulric, entirely belonging to Count Ulric of Ultimis; the sons of Karl of Tisens; Lady Ita with four sons, who belong by half to Count Egenonus; Federicus Nonerius in full, with nine sons, whose sons belong by half to the Crown; the sons of Ulric of Lugagnano; Tristanus, who belongs by half to the Count of Tyrol; Heinrich Nonerius and his sister; Herbert Fulchinerius and his sister Gesam; Bertold of Tisens with three sons; the sons of Riprandus of Lugugnano and two sisters; Calocus of Ultimis, his mother, and his brother Ulric; the wife of Conrad of Senano with four sons; Goteliaba and her daughter with five sons; and Gabardus of Hoenfiain and his sister with three sons.

Many other people together with their households follow; only their names are listed: Nicolaus of Castrorupto; Henricus of Inlander; Galochus of Felsecu; Odescalcus of Monte; N. of Falvenstain; Arnold of Valvenstain; Lord Yra; Arnold of Gaso; Heinrich Chirkerus; Otto Pairus; Hengelmarius; the brothers Heinrich of Milderos; Bertaidus of Obernunc; Conrad of Sarentino; Diamota; Heinrich and the wife of Federicus of Louzo; Liabardus of Jovo; the wife of Bertold of Coredo; Oluradinus of Spur; Wilelmus of Alolina; Egeno of Sillo; Federicus and Sophia; the wife of Arnold of Arso; da Selo; the wife of Adelpret of Flaono; and Heinrich the German.

He also named and specified others of a different status, namely, mazinates: Giobizinus of Mez; Zavarisaus of Mez; Ropertus of Tueno; Ubertinus and his brother Ottonellus of Tunno; Anselmus of Spuro; Conradus of Man; Girardus and Janetinus of Spuro; Engenosus of Loverno; Jordanus of Molar; Bontempno; Zuco and Paganelus of Mula; Zufus Albus, son of Miliolus; Otto of Amblo; Delesmannus of Cloz; Harmanus and Todeschus of Clouz; Provitalis of Cornalezo; Swicherius of Caldaro; Vitalis of Tobolino; Bertold of Teseno; Ulric of Tesino; the son of Ulric the priest and his two sisters; Mairus of Maio; Folcus of Maio; Ysegrinus of Zermo; Conrad of Agino; and others. All the aforesaid people, together with all their children and descendants, male and female, present and future, are included.

These are the Count’s vassals from his allodial holdings whom he assigned: Suppanus; Tarantus; the sons of Engelmar of Tarant; Albero and his brother of Mais; Ylteprandus of Lugugnano; Otto of Tisen; Duringus and his brothers of Formiano; Gotschalchus of Winec; Ulric of Haselach and his brother; Hiltepold and his brother of Winec; Otto of Winec; the sons of the late Jalf; Heinrich of Fossato; Heinrich of Goldeco; Heinrich Kircherius; Enricus of Goldec; Gotsalcus of Falvenfiain; Gotsalcus of Griso and his brother Heinrich Tudes; the sons of Federicus of San Genesio; Heinrich of Fouticello; the sons of Adelpret of Sarentino; Liabardus of Jovo; Liabardus of Vbernum; Jacobus and his brother of Formiano; Folchemarius of Caminata; Feudus, whose fief lies at Mais; Swicherus of Montalban; Hugo of Richenberch; Roser, whose fief lies at Mais; Sibant, whose fief lies at Marling; Otto of Schrofenstein, whose fief lies at Mais; those of Porgchirch, whose fief lies above Maio; the sons of Adelpret of Lugagnano; those of Enno; Nicolaus and his nephews of Egna; Jacobus of Lizana; Abrianus of Castrobarco; Arnold of Arso; the sons of Heinrich of Cloz; Heinrich of Glomio; those of Werneco, whose fief lies at Zermo; those of Rodanch, whose fief lies partly at Caldaro; Wilhelm of Velturno, whose fief lies at Caldaro; and Walmann zu Rosenberg, whose fief lies at Mais.

The following properties are sold. Twenty-eight manses at Caverlana, yielding one hundred pounds annually. At Cadrano, one mansus yielding eight pounds in rent, together with the Sunday court in the castle, yielding five pounds, and the houses below the mountain with meadows, which must maintain thirty-six cows every year. At Ralo, eight manses, yielding twenty-eight pounds annually. At Cloz, six manses, yielding sixteen pounds in rent. At Lugagnano, two manses, yielding thirty pounds annually. At Riader in Grello, two manses, yielding thirty marks annually. At Halles, one mansus, yielding thirty pounds annually. At Hobeniga, one mansus; at Dosso, one mansus; at Castenego, one mansus; two houses and one scaria at Vindria; and seven manses at San Valentino; the annual yield of these manses, the scaria, and the houses is sixteen marks. The Countess shall receive the revenues of those marks for her lifetime. At Zermo, one mansus yielding fifty pounds annually. At Mais, one mansus yielding two hundred pounds annually. At Plaza, three manses yielding thirty pounds. Also the entire allod which he holds at Ultimis, yielding eighty pounds a year.

If any other properties of the noble mazinates or other mazinates, or any other allodial holdings not named here, are found to belong to the aforesaid Count within the Bishopric, Duchy, and District, they are included as well. The Count enfeoffed the aforesaid Lord Bishop and his successors with all these properties by right of sale, as with those listed above, but retained for himself the mansus of Srechpuhel and what he holds at Nova. The Count’s wife shall have the revenues, measured by the weight of Caverlana, from Fiemo for her lifetime only, and the Count may dispose of those revenues as he would his own property.

The Count made these grants, transfers, donations, and enfeoffments to the Bishopric of Trent and to Lord Bishop Gerard, who receives them for his bishopric, on the following terms: henceforth the said bishop and his successors shall hold the aforesaid allods, mazinates, and persons belonging to the mazinates, with their children, present and future, their movable goods and possessions; the casaticas with their possessions, movable goods, and descendants; and the vassals with the fiefs they hold. The bishop may do whatever he wishes with these for the bishopric, without opposition or molestation by the aforesaid Count or anyone else. The Count declares that he has not sold, alienated, or pledged any of the aforesaid properties to anyone other than the Bishop and the Bishopric. If any of them are found to have been alienated or pledged, the Count shall be liable under a mortgage of all his present and future property for twice the value of the property lost or encumbered.

The Count declared that he possessed the aforesaid mazinates, with their movable goods, people, possessions, and the households of the people, on behalf of the Bishop and Bishopric, and ceased to possess them for his own account when forbidden to do so. The Count acknowledged that he had received from the Bishop one thousand pounds of Veronese denarii. By reason of this sale he renounced the defense that the money had not been paid; and if the sale were worth more than that price, he donated the excess to the Bishop, as an irrevocable gift between the living and for the salvation of his soul and those of his parents. He renounced the law which says that a gift is not valid above five hundred gold coins, and every other law by which the gift could be revoked. The Count promised to warrant and defend all the aforesaid properties for the Bishop, on penalty of paying double the value of any property lost and all damages and expenses thereby incurred by the Bishopric.

Immediately thereafter, the Bishop took possession of his mazinates through Lord Ulric the Seneschal of Castelvecchio, Heinrich of Morito, and Johannes Bisólo, who received possession on behalf of the other properties, vassals, and mazinates. Heinrich, Viridis, and Johannes Bisólas immediately swore fealty to the lord Bishop and the Bishopric, as men of the macinata of Saint Vigilius.

The Count made these sales, donations, and enfeoffments on this condition: if the Count should die without sons or daughters, the sales and donations shall remain freely with the Bishopric. If, however, the Count should have sons or daughters, the Bishop or his successor shall have the choice: if he so wishes, the sales, donations, and enfeoffments shall immediately become void and return freely to the Count and his children. The Count or his daughter, as the case may be, must repay four thousand pounds of the aforesaid price within a year from the time the Bishop, his successors, or their messengers notify them.

If the Bishop or his successor so wishes, the sales and enfeoffments may instead remain in force until the Count’s children reach puberty: the sons at fourteen years and the daughters at twelve. If all the children are still minors when the Count dies—that is, before the sons reach fourteen and the daughters twelve—the sales and donations shall remain valid. But if all who survive him have reached puberty at the time of the Count’s death, the sales and donations shall be void and remain with one or more of his children, who must repay the aforesaid four thousand pounds of the price within a year, and so forth. If the Count, or his sons or daughter after his death, as described above, fail to repay the four thousand pounds within the specified period, the Bishop may and shall take possession of everything the Count appears to hold in the parish of Zermo and in the judicary district.

The Count promised that he would not obtain letters from the Supreme Pontiff, the Emperor, the King, or anyone else on account of this pledge, but would leave the Bishop and Bishopric in peace. Furthermore, under a mortgage of all his property, the Count promised the Bishop that he would have his most illustrious wife approve and confirm all the foregoing in the present instrument by the next Feast of Candlemas, and his mother likewise by the next Feast of Saint Martin.

I, Muso, notary of Lord Otto, King of the Romans, was present at all these proceedings and, at the request of the parties, wrote them up in agreement with the notaries Uluradinus and Peregrinus and drew up this public instrument.
